2026-08-01
There's often talk about humans not being able to keep up with all the code produced by LLMs, because things can move so fast now,
hence we need to shift our focus and work differently. To some degree, that is true, we now have the possibility to focus more on
ideation, iteration, verification etc. but the statement is also flawed in a fundamental way.
It is true we can produce enormous amounts of output in a short time using LLMs. However, I believe the old truths still old.
Keep it small and focused, avoid accidental complexity, when something has stabilized, make sure it is well-tested and avoid churn.
I believe that it takes more work to produce smaller and more focused output, just as in writing prose. I also believe that is why LLMs default
to more rather than less output. It's simply more work to achieve the same result using less words.
So, I think we should strive to keep up with the LLM output and understand what is being built, and we should use the LLMs to drive us towards
that clean and clear implementation faster, since we can iterate and refactor many times quicker now than before.
The result is not only good for human understanding, but also for LLM understanding, and by extension, token usage and context quality.

Subagents are the wrong approach.

2026-07-25
== 15:00 ==
People talk about loops, in loosely defined ways.
I think what we are doing is what we have always done, but with more automation. Software development workflows.
Linka is a way to store, in a strict way, our expectations, goals, and implementation process, in an immutable way.
That way we can enter ideas and designs, end goals, and trigger workflows to implement them, and importantly,
analyze if some implementation actually reached a goal.

Another point. Linka may offer some way of tracking ROI of agentic development, and guidance on token spend optimization.
We can get metrics for specific files, or overall features, how much churn they've been through.
And, how much of that churn was based on testing and redesign, relative models performing bad work.
If a human does some implementation work, we can also get metrics on the error rate/code churn of that relative agentic implementation.

== 20:46 ==

I think we should use LLM tools only specifically for the thing they are needed for, and any task
which can be performed with a deterministic tool should be.
An agent shouldn't create branches and worktrees, an LLM can be asked for the name of it.

I think the idea of "Skills" is strange, since either they are snippets that we put in a session, which can be useful.
Otherwise they should be actual commands we run in the environment, not something we tell the agent to do.
If I want a new task created from current context, I should not "use the create new work" skill.
I should run a command which creates the task, and gets the description from the LLM.


2026-07-11
Things have gone a bit crazy.
The core functionality should be a work tracking graph, similar to beads but with much more
structure and verifiability. It should allow the kind of historical view of the work that is mentioned in other documents.

Performing work using that graph is a separate issue, and the review flow is part of that.
That is me wanting a better way to interact with agents, and having a tool to process work in the graph with.
This is essentially my own harness, but where work does not happen through a chat interface, but instead only based on some
task store.
This should be a tool that can use, and benefit from, the linka core, but should technically be fully functional with any kind
of store. It just needs to have some abstraction for where to put things like agent interactions, review notes etc. and some way of getting
information on what work to do, and register completion or failures.

Worktrees are a followup concern altogether, and only relevant for concurrent work.
Otherwise branches are fine.
We shold leave this for last, when single-worker/multi-branch workflow works.
